extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the America Invents Act (AIA) 35 U.S.C. 102(a) and (b) to determine prior art, exceptions, effective filing dates, and related examination procedures when evaluating patentability (novelty) of claimed inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) general prior art rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A person shall be entitled to a patent unless the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; or described in an issued patent or published application naming another inventor and effectively filed before the claimed invention's effective filing date (102(a)(1) and 102(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office bears the initial burden of explaining why statutory/regulatory requirements are not met when rejecting a claim. The categories set forth in 102(a)(1) and (a)(2) are used to determine novelty/nonobviousness; (a)(1) references include patents, published applications, and printed publications and public uses/sales/availability; (a)(2) references are U.S. patent documents only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date of the claimed invention (35 U.S.C. 100(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date is the earliest of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent/application containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent/application is entitled to priority/benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365, or 386.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine effective filing date claim-by-claim. Special situations: (A) continuation/divisional with proper 120/365/386(c) benefit — earliest date in line; (B) continuation-in-part — claims unsupported by parent have filing date of new app, those fully supported take parent's date; (C) provisional benefit under 119(e) — claims fully supported by provisional have provisional date; (D) foreign priority — claims supported by foreign priority doc get foreign filing date. Reissued patents are deemed to have the claim contained in the original patent for effective date purposes. The actual filing date of a national-stage 371 application is the international filing date; international design applications use International Bureau date per Hague rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of patent document prior art by effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of a U.S. patent document as prior art is measured from the effective filing date of the claimed invention, taking into account foreign priority and domestic benefit dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from pre-AIA practice which used either the U.S. application filing date or the applicant's date of invention. Under the AIA the effective filing date governs whether a patent document is prior art to a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim determination of effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective filing date is determined on a claim-by-claim basis rather than an application-by-application basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different claims in the same application may be entitled to different effective filing dates. However, whether to apply pre-AIA or AIA 102/103 is determined application-by-application (see MPEP guidance on applicability).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) — one-year grace period inventor-originated disclosure exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art under 102(a)(1) if (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter (directly/indirectly) from the inventor/joint inventor; or (B) the subject matter had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or another who obtained it from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-year grace period is measured from the filing date of any U.S. or foreign patent application to which the patent/application is entitled to benefit or priority as to such invention (not limited to earliest U.S. filing as pre-AIA). See sections on affidavits/declarations (37 CFR 1.130) for evidentiary procedures to invoke this exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) — exceptions for subject matter in U.S. patent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure shall not be prior art under 102(a)(2) if (A) the subject matter was obtained directly/indirectly from the inventor/joint inventor; (B) the subject matter had before being effectively filed been publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or another who obtained it from them; or (C) the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person by the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102(a)(2) applies to U.S. patent-related documents. The 102(b)(2) exceptions provide analogous protections to 102(b)(1) for these U.S. patent documents and include a common-ownership/assignment prong (b)(2)(C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patented (102(a)(1) — 'patented')
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior patent of a claimed invention will preclude a subsequent patent if the prior patent was granted before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For prior art purposes the applicable prior art date for a patent is its grant date. Exception: secret patents are prior art only from the date they were made available to the public (e.g., laid open for inspection or disseminated in printed form). A U.S. patent that issues after the effective filing date of a claim may still be prior art under 102(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Described in a printed publication (102(a)(1)) — anticipation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent, published patent application, or printed publication may be prior art if it 'describes' the claimed invention — meaning it discloses each and every element of the claimed invention, explicitly or inherently, arranged or combined as in the claim, and provides sufficient guidance to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'described' standard under 102 is the same as pre-AIA. Unlike 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enablement for claims), 102 anticipation need only enable a single species or embodiment to anticipate a broader claim. A prior art document need not disclose 'how to use' the invention for anticipation. A document inadequate for anticipation may still be relied upon under 35 U.S.C. 103 for obviousness for what it reasonably would have made known to a skilled artisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use (102(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use rejections may be based on uses anywhere in the world that made the invention available to the public before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No geographic limitation (contrast pre-AIA 'in this country'). Pre-AIA public use bars required the invention to be ready for patenting and either accessible to the public or commercially exploited; those concepts remain relevant. Uses by the inventor or those who obtained the invention from the inventor may be subject to 102(b)(1) grace period exceptions. When aware of a potential public use, examiners should require applicant info showing it did not make the claimed process accessible to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: On sale (102(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: On sale activity (sales or offers for sale) occurring before the effective filing date may bar patentability regardless of where the sale took place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Pfaff v. Wells: (1) subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (not primarily for experimental purposes), and (2) the invention is ready for patenting. Contract/commercial law principles govern whether a sale/offer occurred. The enablement inquiry is not applicable to the on-sale determination under pre-AIA law (and the phrase 'on sale' is treated similarly under AIA). Sales/uses by the inventor within one year prior to filing may be covered by 102(b)(1) exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Otherwise available to the public (102(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A catch‑all category that includes any disclosure, activity, or circumstance in which the claimed invention was made available to the public before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printed publications that do not have sufficiently early publication dates to qualify themselves as prior art may nevertheless serve as competent evidence that a previous public use, sale, or other public availability occurred at an earlier qualifying date (see In re Epstein).

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement of 'by others' in 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: 102(a)(1) does not require that a use, sale, or other public availability be by another person; inventor-originated disclosures may still be prior art subject to 102(b) exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an activity by the inventor is prior art depends on whether it falls within the 102(b)(1) grace-period exceptions and other factual circumstances (e.g., confidentiality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation vs obviousness application of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art disclosure must satisfy the stricter 'each and every element arranged as in the claim' and enablement for anticipation under 102, but may still be used in an obviousness rejection under 103 for what it would have reasonably taught a skilled artisan even if not anticipatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner may cite a disclosure under 103 for all that it would reasonably have made known; lack of anticipatory detail does not preclude reliance in obviousness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements or admissions by the applicant or inventors can be used as prior art against the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP section on admissions for guidance on when and how admissions constitute disqualifying disclosure and how examiners should treat them in making rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'disclosure' for prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'disclosure' as used in 102 encompasses documents and activities (patents, published applications, printed publications, public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public) that make information about an invention available prior to the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a communication or activity made the subject matter accessible to the public or is attributable to the inventor or another under 102(b) exceptions; see discussion on printed publications, public use, on-sale, and admissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining whether to apply 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the appropriate 102(a) subsection based on the nature of the reference: (a)(1) covers patents, published applications, printed publications, public uses, on sale, otherwise available; (a)(2) covers U.S. patent documents and related published applications where the patent/application names another inventor and was effectively filed earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the type of reference (U.S. patent/published application vs non-patent literature or public activity), effective filing dates for both the reference and the claimed invention, and whether the reference names another inventor. See MPEP §2154 and related sections for details on U.S. patent documents as references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming a 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures and substantive grounds an applicant may use to overcome a prior art rejection under AIA 102(a)(1) or (a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possibilities include showing that the reference does not disclose each and every claim element arranged as claimed, that the prior art is not enabling, asserting applicable 102(b) exceptions with supportive declarations/affidavits under 37 CFR 1.130, demonstrating claim support in earlier priority documents so the effective filing date predates the reference, or showing common ownership/assignment in 102(b)(2)(C). See MPEP §2152.06 and §2155 for detailed affidavit/declaration guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations can be used to overcome prior art rejections by showing that a disclosure was made by the inventor/joint inventor, that the subject matter had been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor, or that another obtained the subject matter from the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP sections detail admissible showing of enablement, who may file an affidavit/declaration, and situations where such affidavits/declarations are unavailable. Examiners should evaluate the sufficiency of the evidence and whether it establishes an applicable 102(b) exception or other grounds to overcome the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership/obligation of assignment (102(b)(2)(C))
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure shall not be prior art under 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person by the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prong is aimed at U.S. patent document references; examiners should assess ownership/assignment relationships and dates to determine whether the common ownership exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antedating/'swearing behind' restricted under AIA
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AIA, effective filing date-based prior art makes it no longer possible to antedate or 'swear behind' certain prior art disclosures by showing the inventor invented prior to the effective date of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because AIA 102(a)(1) and (a)(2) concern disclosures before the effective filing date rather than the date of invention, the traditional pre-AIA practice of antedating via 37 CFR 1.131 is curtailed for references governed by these provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedural requirements when making rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is rejected or an objection/requirement is made, the Office shall notify the applicant and state the reasons, and provide information and references useful to the applicant (35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.104(c), MPEP §706).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate statutory/regulatory grounds for rejection and provide the references/information necessary for applicants to judge whether to continue prosecution. Form paragraphs are provided in the MPEP for common rejection types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs for AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardized form paragraph language is available for use in drafting rejections under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP provides recommended form paragraphs to ensure consistent, complete, and compliant statement of reasons and supporting references in Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability dates and determining FITF coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on which applications are subject to First-Inventor-to-File (FITF) AIA provisions versus pre-AIA rules, and how to determine which set of rules (pre-AIA or AIA) applies to particular claimed inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2159 and related subsections for detailed rules about applications filed before/after March 16, 2013, transition applications, and how to treat claimed inventions with effective filing dates on either side of the cutoff.
